read.text: WEANING FROM MECHANICAL VENTILATION:

• This process should be considered as soon as pulmonary function begins to improve. Decisions concerning weaning are separate and apart from decisions concerning extubation.
  • During weaning from mechanical ventilation, a patient gradually takes on more of the function of gas exchange while the ventilator contributes less to the patient’s minute ventilation.
  • The circumstances that required mechanical ventilation support must be resolved. In addition, the patient must actively participate in the process, and objective and subjective criteria must be set to monitor the success or failure of the process.
  • Factors that influence weaning from mechanical ventilation include:
    • the patient’s level of alertness,
    • need for sedative medication,
    • respiratory drive and adequacy of oxygenation (SPO2 >95% with fractional excretion of oxygen< 40% and or low PEEP requirements <7cmH2o),
    • Adequacy of ventilation (PaCo2 <45 mmHg with no chronic respiratory failure, or >45 mmHg with acceptable PH),
    • the time elapsed since the patient’s most recent episode of respiratory or hemodynamic decompensation.
  • Although previously thought of as a failed weaning attempt, it is currently endorsed by the American College of Chest Physicians and the American Thoracic Society (ATS) to extubate patients to preventive non-invasive ventilation. Multiple studies correlated extubation to NIV with shorter intensive care length of stay and short-term mortality. Predictors for successful extubation:
  • Once the neonate has achieved ventilatory settings when extubation seems to be a reasonable next step, physicians should evaluate whether the patient is ‘ready’ or not for extubation. This is a very important phase of this whole process since some patients can be easily weaned to low settings but are not yet prepared to cope with respiration without invasive support.
  • The following section will review the role of clinical factors, spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) and autonomic nervous system function evaluation in assessing extubation readiness in extremely preterm infants.
Clinical Factors:Several epidemiological studies have tried to identify the risk factors
associated with extubation failure in preterm infants. Those include:

• low gestational age (<26 weeks),
    • prolonged ventilation (>10–14 days),
    • low pH and extubation from high ventilatory settings (e.g., high mean airway pressure and high FiO₂ ).
    • Infants with a history of previous extubation failure or multiple intubation attempts are also predisposed to fail extubation again.
    • In addition, the presence of other morbidities, such as residual lung disease (e.g., bronchopulmonary dysplasia) or a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) can increase the likelihood of extubation failure.
  • Autonomic Nervous System Function :
    • Variations in heart rate and respiratory rate are well known to be influenced by the autonomic nervous system (ANS). In fact, integrity of the cardiovascular system depends on the right balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic tones.
    • The role of heart rate variability(HRV) and respiratory variability(RV) in predicting disease in newborn infants is not as well understood.
    • It has however gained popularity over the past years, especially with the latest evidence that loss of HRV precedes the clinical presentation of late-onset neonatal sepsis.
    • With regards to prediction of extubation readiness, a recent small prospective observational study of 56 preterm infants (birth weight ≤1,250 g) showed that HRV was significantly decreased in those who failed extubation.
Which preterm babies are at higher risk of failing extubation?
read.answer: Low gestational age (< 26 weeks), prolonged ventilation (> 10–14 days), low pH, extubation from high settings (high MAP, high FiO₂), previous extubation failure or multiple intubation attempts, and residual lung disease (BPD) or a significant PDA.

read.text: Spontaneous Breathing Trials

• SBTs have been validated and extensively used in adult and pediatric patients as a means of predicting successful extubation.
  • In premature infants, though, data to justify their use are insufficient. A meta-analysis on SBT concluded that preterm infants should be extubated directly without a trial of SBT.
    • permissive hypercapnia is a strategy that may facilitate weaning from MV and reduce ventilator-induced lung injury.
    • Various PaCO₂ targets have been used in studies, although generally they are limited by a pH of at least 7.20–7.25.
    • Preterm infants exposed to permissive hypercapnia for 10 days or longer have shown improved respiratory drive, a reduction in number of days on MV, and a trend toward reduction of BPD or death. It appears suitable to target PaCO₂ levels of 50–60 while maintaining a pH over 7.20
PRACTISE THIS SKILL How to Extubate:

• Once an infant is deemed ready for extubation, a number of steps need to be followed methodically to ensure a successful transition.
  • The process of extubation takes time, meticulous planning and requires the full collaboration of all team members caring for the infant (including clinicians, nurses and respiratory therapists). The procedure itself should be done in a controlled environment, in the presence of personnel skilled in respiratory stabilization and intubation (if needed)
  • 1. Develop and implement a mechanical ventilation protocol, including the weaning phase, extubation and reintubation criteria. This should involve all health care professionals (neonatologists, nurses and respiratory therapists)
working at the NICU.

• 2. Use assist control mode with volume-targeted ventilation if equipped with the proximal flow sensor
  • 3. Allow for permissive hypercapnia (PaCO₂ 50–60 mmHg) and establish oxygen saturation targets (SpO₂ 91–95 %)
  • 4. Administer a loading dose of caffeine before extubation (ideally within 24 h prior to extubation)
  • 5. Place the infant on CPAP or NIPPV immediately after extubation (PEEP ≥5 cmH O) using bi-nasal prongs or a nasal mask
  • 6. Enteral feeds should be stopped for 4 hrs before extubation.
  • 7. Acceptable weaning parameters may include:
  • i. MAP 8cm H2o or less,
  • ii. Fio2 less than 30-40%
  • iii. Rate less than 30Bpm with acceptable blood gas
Use of Caffeine Prior to Extubation
• The benefits of caffeine for extremely preterm infants have been suggested in several small single-center studies and confirmed by a large multi-center trial conducted in.
This randomized controlled trial showed that infants assigned to the caffeine group had less BPD, a shorter duration on supplemental oxygen and were intubated for almost 1 week less.

• A secondary, post hoc subgroup analysis showed that early administration of caffeine (before 3 days of life) could further reduce the time on MV
  • From these studies, we conclude that caffeine is beneficial and should be part of the regimen when preparing an infant for extubation. It appears reasonable to give it within at least 24 h from the projected time of extubation. However, although tempting, the routine administration of caffeine immediately after birth (or in the first few hours after birth) has not been investigated.
After extubating a preterm baby, when is CPAP or NIPPV started?
options: After 4 hours if the baby tires
Only if a blood gas is abnormal
Not needed if caffeine was given

read.text: Post-extubation Ventilation Strategies

• Following extubation, premature infants still have insufficient respiratory drive and muscle strength to maintain FRC independently. For this reason, a distending pressure is necessary to reduce the risk of post-extubation atelectasis. This pressure should be applied immediately after the removal of the endotracheal tube and may be provided in the form of CPAP or nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) using short, bi-nasal prongs or nasal masks.
Common reasons for failed weaning include:

• Cardiac dysfunction
  • Cognitive dysfunction
  • Respiratory pump failure
  • Respiratory muscle and diaphragmatic dysfunction
  • Metabolic disorders
A baby keeps failing extubation. What does the manual list as common reasons for failed weaning?
options: Cardiac or cognitive dysfunction, respiratory pump failure, respiratory muscle and diaphragm dysfunction, metabolic disorders
read.explanation: Look beyond the lungs: the heart, metabolic state, diaphragm and sedation.

read.text:
• Mechanical ventilation (MV) is life-saving for many babies who require respiratory support in the newborn period.
  • Paediatric patients and newborns in particular are anatomically and physiologically than the increase in airway diameter which is a precipitating factor in why infants are especially prone to hyperinflation and air trapping.
  • Unfortunately, infants who require mechanical ventilation frequently develop complications. The most common ones are:
  • A. Lung injury and oxygen toxicity:
    • 1. BPD is related to increased airway pressure and changes in lung volume, although
oxygen toxicity, anatomic and physiologic immaturity, and individual susceptibility also contribute.
• 2. Air leak is directly related to increased airway pressure. Risk is increased at MAPs in
excess of 14 cm H2O.

• B. Mechanical:
    • 1. Obstruction of endotracheal tubes may result in hypoxemia and respiratory acidosis.
    • 2. Equipment malfunction, particularly disconnection, is not uncommon and requires
functioning alarm systems and vigilance.

• C. Complications of invasive monitoring:
    • 1. Peripheral arterial occlusion with infarction
    • 2. Aortic thrombosis from umbilical arterial catheters, occasionally leading to renal
impairment and hypertension
• 3. Emboli from flushed catheters, particularly to the lower extremities, the splanchnic bed,
or even the brain

• D. Anatomic:
    • 1. Subglottic stenosis from prolonged intubation; risk increases with multiple reintubations
    • 2. Acquired tracheobronchomalacia from prolonged mechanical intubation
    • 3. Palatal grooves from prolonged orotracheal intubation
    • 4. Vocal cord damage
  • E. Ventilator associated pneumonia caused by nosocomial infection in the NICU. It can be prevented by early extubation to minimize the time spent on the ventilator, changing ventilator circuits only as needed, mouth care, and medical staff hand hygiene.
How can ventilator-associated pneumonia be prevented, according to the manual?
options: Early extubation, changing circuits only as needed, mouth care and hand hygiene

• Sudden desaturation with high CO2: Disconnect the patient and bag;
    • If he improves, then check the ventilator (O2 source, increase Fio2, consider mechanical or electrical failure).
    • Also check the tube for displacement, obstruction or Leak.
    • If he does not improve, now assess the baby for pneumothorax, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, intraventricular haemorrhage and sepsis.
  • Gradual desaturation with high CO2: This suggests inappropriate ventilator settings;
    • Increase PIP/ PEEP/ I:E ratio
    • Repeat blood gas.
  • Gradual increase in PCO2 without gross changes in PO2: May be due to:
    • Insufficient tidal volume, rate or both
    • Increased dead space (long ETT, non-ventilated alveoli)
Actions:

• Increase PIP by (2-5cm water), and/ or
    • Decrease PEEP by 1, and/ or
    • Increase rate by (5-10 bpm), and/ or
    • Shorten ETT if long to decrease the dead space.
  • Decrease in PCO2 caused by over-ventilation:
        • Decrease the rate,
        • Decrease PIP and or increase PEEP.
A ventilated baby suddenly desaturates with a high CO₂. What is the first action?
options: Disconnect the baby from the ventilator and bag by hand
Increase the FiO₂ on the ventilator
Send a blood gas and wait

exercises.source: Manual Module (3) Intensive Newborn Care, Section 2 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 7719)
narrative: 30 minutes after CPAP initiation: RR 62/min · HR 148/min · SpO₂ 92% on FiO₂ 0.30 · chest indrawing mild · baby more active.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: IMPROVEMENT. Compare to a distressed baby: the rate has settled, the indrawing is now only mild, the baby is more active, and the saturation is on target at a LOW FiO₂ of 0.30. Every trend is the right way.
The parameters that prove it: reduced work of breathing (mild indrawing), a settling respiratory rate, improved activity — not the saturation alone.
Document: the settings, the full set of vitals, the work of breathing, and the time.
Plan: continue CPAP, maintain monitoring, avoid unnecessary changes.

Teaching point: this is the GREEN column of the traffic light. The instinct of an anxious team is to keep adjusting a baby who is getting better. Do not. ‘Avoid unnecessary changes’ is an active decision, not passivity.
The CPAP Adjustment Traffic Light (Module 3) INCREASE CPAP INCREASE FiO₂ NO CHANGE
For every 10% FiO₂ rise: reassess need for 1 cmH₂O CPAP increase
The golden rule of adjustment: FiO₂ and pressure go hand in hand. If there is a mismatch, something is wrong. Bring down the FiO₂ FIRST, then the pressure.

Monitoring — What You Check, and How Often Frequency Check EVERY HOUR (visual) The nose is not squashed or pushed upwards · the eyes are clearly visible · tapes not too tight, no indentation, pitting or ocular oedema At least 4-HOURLY (physical) Hat fit — not too tight/loose, not rubbing · remove prongs/mask to rest the nose from pressure · inspect the nose for redness, breakdown, bruising, indentation, altered shape, bleeding · prongs clean and patent before replacing · ears not creased or folded Continuously Pulse oximetry · HR, RR, chest indrawing, grunting, flaring As required Blood gas · regular inspection of the circuit and equipment
Remember (manual): remove prongs/mask by LOOSENING the tapes, not by pulling them off the face. Perform regular mouth care. Suctioning should NOT be routine — only as the baby dictates.
Document whenever the nose is checked.
Also monitor: capillary refill, blood pressure, urine output; tone, activity and response; a respiratory distress score (e.g. Downe's); chest X-ray at start and if deterioration occurs.
Babies are initially kept nil per mouth until stabilised.
Thereafter, commence feeds by orogastric tube.

points: CPAP has failed. Three criteria met: FiO₂ now > 0.6; pH < 7.28 with PaCO₂ > 60; recurrent apnoea requiring stimulation. This is not a borderline call.

Next step: intubation and invasive ventilation. Before touching a dial — the intubation itself (taught in the Advance Airway session), confirmed tube position, and a plan. HFNC during intubation improves first-attempt success and stability (cross-reference NIV).
Surfactant: this RDS baby who is now intubated should receive surfactant — early rescue. The ventilator and the surfactant are one decision, not two (cross-reference Prematurity — RDS).
